newsitem.title: USA: Pennsylvania town scarred by TWA crash.
newsitem.headline: Pennsylvania town scarred by TWA crash.

text.p: The year has passed quickly since TWA Flight 800 blew up and killed his daughter Cheryl, and the pain is still raw for Don Nibert.
Others in this tiny Pennsylvania town say the tragedy which took 21 of its members will leave a lasting scar.
"It doesn't seem that a year has passed," Nibert said in an interview, his voice reflecting the hurt, anger and other emotions that have buffeted him over the last 12 months.
"When this happened, I thought a grievance process of two to three months would be adequate. We've gone through a year, and it hasn't been," he said.
"I think we have progressed fairly well," he said, referring also to his wife, Donna. However, he said, "I really don't think that my wife and I will ever fully recover."

Cheryl Nibert and 15 other members of the French club at the Montoursville High School, along with five adult chaperones, were killed in crash of TWA 800. The plane exploded off Long Island on July 17, 1996, shortly after it left New York for Paris. All 230 people aboard died.
The town, many of whose 5,000 residents had some connection to the crash victims, was devastated.

The dead are remembered with flowers of blue and gold -- the high school colours -- in planters along the main street and in private gardens, with ribbons hung from porches, and with silent visits to the gravesites of 17 of victims grouped on a hilltop overlooking the riverside town.
Some residents, relatively distant from the tragedy, have returned to life as before.

"The tragedy is not the main conversation any more," Mayor John Dorin said. "About six months down the line I started seeing that. To me that was one way of telling me that the community was on its way to healing."
However, he said, "I don't think our town will ever be back to normal. I think Montoursville will always be identified with that tragedy."

A group of Montoursville clergy organised a remembrance service for Thursday evening at the high school gym. The service will be in memory of the TWA victims and other residents who died under tragic circumstances in recent years.
Parents of the crash victims continue meeting in bi-weekly support groups, although attendance has slipped, Nibert said.
"I am very proud of the men. The first thing we had to get over was the John Wayne image -- men don't cry. And we overcame that," Nibert said.

Parents have also been involved in committees to build a memorial -- a site was recently chosen near the high school -- and to administer a scholarship fund. The memorial and scholarship funds have grown with contributions from around the world to more than $700,000, Dorin said.

Nibert, who said he was angered by insensitive media handling of the tragedy, spoke at two forums on press treatment of disasters. "My anger has been more directed to the news media han anyone else," he said.

Nibert and Will Rogers, whose only child, Kimberly, died in the crash, said one of the many emotions they had to deal with was a sense of personal failure. "I unfortunately let her out of my sight once too often," Rogers said.
The approach of the year's passage since the crash has heightened the pain, Nibert said. But he would not characterise the date as an anniversary.
"My use of that word usually denotes a pleasurable event -- a wedding anniversary," he said. "There's nothing pleasurable about this event, or anything that would bring joy."
Rogers said, for him, each day of the past year "has been just about the same."
"We manage to make ourselves appear better now in public, but we still feel the same inside, we still hurt," he said.
